catalog_citation: Petzell, Malin. 2002. A sketch of Kimwani (a minority language of Mozambique). Africa & Asia 2: 88-110. Göteborg: Dept of Oriental and African Languages, Göteborg University. (Journal PDF via web.archive.org(.)
catalog_locator: Section 2 'Phonology and orthography', pp. 91-92; also Section 1 p. 89 and Section 3.3 (verb morphology) on tone in SM sets / past tense
catalog_quote: As for pitch, Kimwani has movable pitch accent (Nurse & Hinnebusch, 1993: 524). Philippson in Nurse & Hinnebusch (1993: 256) has several complicated rules that will not be dealt with here. Kimwani does not have the penultimate stress common in Kiswahili and its variants. In addition, I have seen no evidence that Kimwani is a tone language, but Philippson reports (pc June-00) that tone is distinctive in some verb paradigms. ... [p.89] However, they cannot explain why Kimwani has some prosodic features from the neighbouring languages such as Shimakonde. ... [3.3] It is sometimes problematic to tell if the ku is a SM or a prefix to the stem in the short verbs (cl.15). The tones are the distinctive elements in this case. Set one (ku) has a low tone which distinguishes it from the infinitive prefix cl.15 (Philippson, pc June-00). ... According to Nurse & Hinnebusch, the pitch pattern differs…

tone_statements.citation: Devos, Maud & Salimo Calawia. 2017. Mwani verb tone. Africana Linguistica 23: 167-214. DOI 10.2143/AL.23.0.3256924 (open access, Peeters Online Journals).
tone_statements.quote: The mora is the tone bearing unit in Mwani. It can be either high (/H/) or toneless (/Ø/). Tone assignment rules and phonological tone rules in Mwani only refer to /H/. Moreover, an important restriction on the distribution of tones in Mwani, i.e., no initial /H/ (Section 2.4), only concerns /H/. These facts ... point towards a tone system with privative H (cf. Hyman 2001 and references therein). The absence of contour tones on short vowels is in line with such an analysis. Surface contours are found on long vowels and are analysed as combinations of /H/ and /Ø/.
tone_statements.summary: Privative H vs toneless per mora (count 1 = H only); nouns PU-H or APU-H melody, verbs no lexical tone but 3 inflectional melodies; authors reject 'pitch accent', call lexical tone restricted.

tone_statements.summary: Gives a placement rule the catalog entry lacks (catalog: tonal / pitch accent, no rule): every nominal has H on the stem-initial (radical) syllable, and stems of more than three syllables also get an H on the penultimate; the author calls this a hybrid between the radical-syllable and penultimate types and says more descriptive work is needed. Data credited to Philippson 1989 (author's own).

audit.recode_to: No change of kind (stays tonal / tonal-OR-pitch accent, not fixed stress). Rewrite the primary-stress rule from Devos & Calawia 2017 §2.1-2.3: two-tone (H vs Ø) system, mora = TBU; nouns carry a single obligatory, culminative H on the penultimate or antepenultimate mora (lexically split ~50/50), verbs have no lexical tone but tense-assigned melodic H (can be all-L or have two H peaks); no automatic phrase-final penultimate lengthening; dialects differ prosodically (Floor 2010 App. E: KiWibu antepenult vs northern penult in trisyllabic infinitives; KiNsimbwa 'closer to Swahili').
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: every sentence of the deciding quotation is verbatim in the Petzell 2002 PDF we hold at the stated places (pp. 91-92 across the page break, p. 89, §3.3). (2) The deciding source is a 23-pp working-paper sketch whose prosody statement is second-hand (Nurse & Hinnebusch 1993; Philippson pc) and explicitly omits the rules; Petzell even writes she saw 'no evidence that Kimwani is a tone language'. Better sources exist and two were open: Devos & Calawia 2017 (48-pp tone article, Africana Linguistica, open access at Peeters) and Floor 2010 (SIL sketch with a Tone chapter, open at Frankfurt), both now with a manifest. sources.quote: 'Mwani has been described as a pitch-accent language (Philippson 1989, 1992, 1993) mainly because of the prosodic properties of its nouns. Mwani nouns share three properties which are typically considered accentual ...: culminativity, obligatoriness and demarcativeness. There are no entirely low nouns ... Instead the majority of nouns have a single H tone which surfaces on the penultimate (PU) or antepenultimate (APU) mora ... Mwani verbs, however, are less accent-like. sources.citation: Devos, Maud & Salimo Calawia. 2016. Mwani melodic tones. Handout, Workshop 6 (Melodic tones in Bantu), Bantu 6 conference, Helsinki.
sources.quote: 'Philippson (1989, 1992 & 1993) describes Mwani as a pitch-accent language with movable pitch-accent ... Mwani nouns clearly have all three properties [culminativity, demarcativeness, obligatoriness]' (nouns with PU H vs APU H); 'Mwani verbs are less accent-like ... the current description appeals to tone not accent'; 'basic two tone system with High and Low tones. Only H tones are underlyingly present; mora is the TBU'; four main dialects 'with prosodic differences'; H assignment restricted to word level (citing Philippson 1993: 248-258).

sources.citation: Floor, Sebastian. 2010. Mwani grammatical sketch (Gramática de Kimwani). Primeira edição electrónica. Nampula: SIL Moçambique. 73 pp. urn:nbn:de:hebis:30-112253.
sources.quote: 'Pitch differences, called "tone", are very important in Kimwani. For words of different lengths, there exist different tone "melodies" ... One can make no sense of the verb without understanding the tone differences.' Noun tone patterns tabulated by shape (CV.CV HL/RL/FL, CV.CV.CV LHL/LFL, CV.CV.CV.CV LHLL, 5-syll LLHLL) with a list of exceptions and a few tonal minimal pairs (mfûko 'lazy person' vs mfúko 'bag'); 'Kimwani has no productive lexical tone ... Kimwani does have grammatical tone, that is, tenses are distinguished by tone differences only.' Appendix E: KiWibu/KiKisanga trisyllabic

Nampula: JUWA e SIL Moçambique. 12 pp. (2-up booklet of 24 pp; Glottolog 58682 / SIL 45215: 2002, 20 pp.). Tone lesson 'TOM e ACENTO': p. 5 = booklet p. 20 (índice 'Tom/acento' 18).
sources.note: Lesson 'TOM e ACENTO' (p. 4) consists of nine tone-only minimal sets of inflected verbs written with diacritics, e.g. nîfyoma 'eu tinha lido' / nifyoma 'eu leio, eu li' / nífyoma 'eu hei-de ler'; tîfyoma / tifyóma 'nós (já) lemos' / tífyoma; wakuka 'eles vão' / wakúka 'se eles forem' / wákuka 'eles iam'; ákiwa 'ele era' / akíwa 'se ele for' — showing H placement (prefix vs stem) distinguishing TAM/conditional forms. Data only, no prose analysis; nothing on stress beyond the heading.

sources.note: Per Devos & Calawia 2017 (2.1) this thesis, with Philippson 1989/1993, analyses Mwani as a pitch accent language (nouns culminative: a single H on the penultimate or antepenultimate mora, no all-L nouns). theses.fr abstract: autosegmental-metrical typology of East African Bantu prosodic systems from fully tonal (Kikuyu) to demarcative penultimate accent (Swahili), tonal processes (tone shift, anticipation), tone-syntax domains, and Common Bantu tonal correspondences per language, with the hypothesis that emergent penultimate accent drove the evolution. The Mwani pages themselves not seen.
